Alexander Fleming. The Scottish bacteriologist who discovered penicillin in 1928 through the chance observation of a contaminating mould that inhibited bacterial growth. His finding launched the antibiotic era and saved countless lives from bacterial infection.

Fleming's key discovery came when a mould colony called Penicillium notatum contaminated a bacterial culture plate and lysed surrounding Staphylococcus colonies. It was a moment where serendipity met an observant mind. He worked at St. Mary's Hospital in London for most of his career, and it was there that he made not only this landmark discovery but also identified the enzyme lysozyme found in tears and saliva.

What made penicillin remarkable was that it killed bacteria without immediately poisoning mammalian cells. This was exactly the kind of selective antimicrobial that Paul Ehrlich had envisioned years earlier as a magic bullet. However, Fleming struggled to isolate and stabilise penicillin. It was only through the wartime effort of Howard Florey and Ernst Boris Chain that penicillin was purified and manufactured at scale. Fleming remained humble about his role, calling penicillin a lucky find, but his preparation and keen eye made him the fortunate recipient of that luck.

His discovery prompted the systematic search for antibiotics from microorganisms, leading to streptomycin, tetracycline, and countless others that followed. In 1945, Fleming shared the Nobel Prize with Florey and Chain, the men who turned his observation into a clinically viable drug that transformed medicine.
